_comment: The English catalogue. Every string is transcribed from the approved click dummy, which owns the words as well as the layout, EXCEPT the pending.* block - that declares an unbuilt screen and is new app-side copy. GATE 4 was granted on 2026-09-05 and the 38 approved changes are in the dummy; the ones that touch a screen this app has built are reflected here. A change is written into the dummy first and copied here second, never the other way round.

theme.title: Appearance
home.heroSubMeasured_one: measured {{count}} minute ago across {{targets}} targets in {{sections}} sections
home.heroSubMeasured_other: measured {{count}} minutes ago across {{targets}} targets in {{sections}} sections
home.heroSubUnmeasured: Nothing has been measured yet. A scan reads sizes and deletes nothing.
home.safeRunTitle: A safe run, step by step
home.developerOn: On – keeping anything used in the last {{days}} days
home.developerOff: Off – every cache is offered in full
home.developerNote: Caches you have used recently are left alone, so your next build is not a cold one.
home.idleWindowHint: Lower it to include more caches.
home.assure: Your documents, photos, keys and saved passwords are never touched — whatever you click here.
home.privacySummary: What leaves this machine, and what never does.
home.privacyIntro: The cleanup engine makes no network calls at all — its own tests check that. The window sends usage and crash reports, which is how windowsweep gets better for everyone:
home.privacySignIn: Signing in is optional. It syncs your settings and a summary of each run, and nothing else.
home.mapTableSummary: The same data as a table
home.mapAria: Reclaim map: {{targets}} targets across {{sections}} sections, {{amount}} reclaimable in total. The equivalent data is in the table below.
home.mapZeroBody: Every location behind these tiles is protected or in use. There is nothing here the scan is willing to touch.
home.mapUnmeasuredBody: A scan reads the size of every declared target and deletes nothing. The map draws what it finds.
home.ladderTotal: Total a safe run would free
home.ladderEmpty: Nothing in the safe batch right now.
home.needsHint: A safe run never touches these — you pick, item by item.
home.chokeBody: Every deletion in the product goes through one function, and that function is given a folder it is allowed to work inside. There is no second route, so a path outside that folder cannot be reached even by mistake.
home.chokeRefusedWhat: Protected, or outside the allowed folder
home.chokeRecycleWhat: Anything personal, so you can get it back
home.chokeDeletedWhat: Caches that rebuild themselves next time you need them
home.sparkAria: Space freed by the last {{count}} runs, oldest first: {{amounts}}.
home.lastRunsEmpty: No run has finished in this window yet.
home.lastRunsEmptyNote: A dry-run costs nothing and deletes nothing, and it is recorded here like any other run.
home.scheduleNote: Runs the safe batch once a week and tells you what it freed. Never the sections that need you.
home.adminSummary_one: {{count}} section needs Windows to ask your permission first.
home.adminSummary_other: {{count}} sections need Windows to ask your permission first.
home.adminBody: Starting one opens a second window with its own log, because this window cannot answer a Windows permission prompt for you. It then follows that run and shows you the result.
home.adminSigning: The installer is not signed with a paid code-signing certificate, so Windows warns you the first time you open it. Saying so here costs less than letting you find out; the Administrator rights screen explains the dialog and what you can check instead.
run.titleFailed: The run stopped before it finished.
run.failedNote: Whatever it had already reclaimed is in the log below, and the last line says why it stopped.
run.dryRunNote: This was a dry-run. Run the same thing without it to reclaim the space.
run.drainHint: Tiles leave as each section finishes
run.provenanceBody: The progress you see is reported by the cleanup engine itself as it works. This window displays it and does none of the deleting.
run.nothingToRun: Nothing in the safe batch to run.
sections.title: Sections
sections.lede: The catalogue is a frozen public contract – a number is never reused, and a retired section becomes a no-op that says so.
sections.reportOnlyTitle: Report only - there is nothing to select
sections.detailReportOnly: This section writes a report and deletes nothing.
sections.detailNothing: Nothing declared on this machine right now.
sections.emptyBody: All {{count}} are still there. The filter is narrow.
sections.policySummary: What the four run policies mean
sections.policyBody: <1>Safe</1> runs on its own. <3>Opt-in</3> only runs if you name it. <5>Deep</5> needs an extra confirmation on top. <7>Interactive</7> needs you to pick the items, one by one.
sections.selBlocked: Sections {{ids}} need you to choose items first. Nothing was run.
consent.title: windowsweep collects usage data to improve the product for everyone.
consent.lede: The cleanup engine makes <1>zero network calls</1> – its own test suite asserts that, and that does not change. What follows is only about the desktop window you are looking at.
consent.provider.ga4.name: Product analytics
consent.provider.ga4.what: Which screens you opened and which buttons you pressed.
consent.provider.amplitude.name: Behaviour analytics
consent.provider.amplitude.what: The same events, kept longer so trends over months are visible.
consent.provider.clarity.name: Session replay
consent.provider.clarity.what: A recording of this window with every piece of text masked.
consent.provider.sentry.name: Crash reports
consent.provider.sentry.what: A stack trace when something breaks, with file paths stripped out.
consent.detailsSummary: What the window sends, in plain terms
consent.neverSent: a file path, a folder name, a drive label, your user name, your machine name, or the contents of anything. A run summary is a count and a number of bytes.
consent.noSwitch: There is no switch for this and no setting to find. This is how windowsweep gets better for the next person who runs it.
pending.title: This screen is specified and not yet translated.
pending.body: The click dummy specifies it in full and this window does not carry it yet. It is named here rather than hidden, so what is missing is a stated gap rather than something you have to discover.
pending.reference: Specified in the click dummy at
pending.mapIdle: Two things the click dummy specifies here are not built: the tiles are not shaded by how long each cache has sat unused, and the table has no Idle column. Both need the scan to report an age per target, and it reports a size only.
pending.mapExclude: Clicking a tile to keep it out of the next run is not built. The engine can exclude a path for one section only, not for the caches this map mostly shows, so a tile you had clicked would still be deleted.
pending.drives: The drive rails and the capacity ring the click dummy specifies here are not built. A run reports what it reclaimed, and nothing about your drives or how much room is left on them, so this window has no measured figure to draw.
pending.protectedChips: The click dummy lists the protected locations here by name. This window does not: the protection is several separate mechanisms inside the engine and it publishes no readable list of them, so a partial list printed here would understate what is actually refused. Run windowsweep --list-targets to read the full list.
pending.schedule: The weekly run cannot be switched on from this window yet. The engine registers the task itself — windowsweep --install-task, Sundays at 03:00, the safe batch — but that is not one of the things this window is allowed to ask it to do.
pending.runCancel: Cancel is not built. Stopping a run once it has started means signalling the engine while it works, and this build has no way to do that. A button that looked like it had cancelled and had not would be worse than one that says so.
pending.runProgress: Each section fills its bar in one step because that is what the engine reports: it says when a section starts and when it ends, never how far through it is. The click dummy's sliding bar is prototype animation over invented phases.
pending.heldBack: How much developer mode is holding back is not measured. A scan reports what each target holds on disk — the engine prints that caveat itself — and nothing in its summary says how much of that the idle gate would keep, so a figure here would be invented. The idle window beside it is real: it is the threshold the next run uses.
common.loading: Reading the catalogue from the engine
error.engineMissing: The cleanup engine did not start. Reinstall windowsweep, or run the command-line tool once to confirm it works.
splash.step.updateNoAnswer: Checking for a newer build… no answer
splash.detailsSummary: What happens while this is on screen
splash.detailsWhat: Three things, none of which touch your disk: the bundled engine reports its version, the catalogue is read from `--list --json` so a new section appears without an app update, and the updater checks whether a newer build exists.
splash.detailsNothing: Nothing is scanned and nothing is deleted until you ask. If the update check cannot reach the network it is skipped and says so - reclaiming space has never needed it.
splash.update.body: Install it now, or carry on and install it later. Your settings and history are untouched either way.
splash.update.offlineTitle: The update check could not reach the network.
splash.update.offlineBody: Skipped - nothing else in windowsweep needs it.
splash.update.retriedOffline: Checked again - still offline. Carrying on without it.
settings.title: Settings
settings.lede: Most of these map to a flag the engine already has, so anything you set here you can also pass on a command line. Privacy is the exception: it states what the window sends rather than setting anything.
settings.noKeys: No destination is configured in this build, so nothing is actually sent from it.
settings.about: windowsweep reclaims disk space on Windows. It names every path before it touches one, and refuses your documents, credentials and browser state outright. The desktop window drives the same engine the command-line tool runs.
history.title: History
history.emptyTitle: windowsweep has not run on this machine yet.
history.emptyBody: A dry-run costs nothing and deletes nothing.
history.signedOutNote: Signed out, so this is this machine only. Signing in brings the runs from your other machines alongside these.
picker.title: Nothing here goes unless you choose it.
picker.lede: A safe run never touches these. The engine offered every row below; the ones you tick are the ones that go, and the rest are left exactly as they are.
picker.emptyBody: The sections that ask a person to choose - stale project artefacts, partial downloads, large idle files in Downloads, orphaned application data - populate this screen when one of them runs.
picker.consequence: The Recycle Bin can be emptied later. Permanent has no undo.
report.emptyBody: A report is written for every run, including a dry-run, and the file on disk says exactly what this screen says.
report.onDisk: The same report, on disk at
account.title: Sign in only if you want your settings on another machine.
account.lede: Reclaiming space is never gated. Signing in moves your settings and a summary of each run between your own machines, and that is all it does.
account.whatSyncs: What syncs, per run: the date, the mode, whether it was a dry-run, whether it was elevated, which section numbers ran, the bytes reclaimed, the bytes a dry-run estimated, how long it took, and an id. Plus your appearance settings, developer mode, and a last-seen timestamp.
account.whatNeverSyncs: What never syncs: a file path, a folder name, a drive label, your machine name or your Windows user name.
account.signOutNote: Signing out clears every local trace of the account, including the rows cached from your other machines.
account.notConfigured: Sign-in is not configured in this build
account.notConfiguredNote: The OAuth client id is absent, so this build cannot sign in. Everything else works exactly the same.
elevation.title: {{count}} sections need Windows to ask your permission.
elevation.lede: windowsweep never elevates itself. When you ask for one of these, it opens a second, elevated window that does that work and writes its own report. This window keeps running, unelevated, and shows you the log as it arrives.
elevation.whatHappens: What happens when you press it
elevation.step.asks.title: Windows asks you.
elevation.step.asks.body: The standard User Account Control prompt, from Windows, not from windowsweep. If you say no, nothing happens and nothing is written.
elevation.step.second.title: A second window opens.
elevation.step.second.body: It runs only the sections you chose, with --reports-dir and --logs-dir pointed at this run’s folder.
elevation.step.tails.title: This window tails the log.
elevation.step.tails.body: You watch it from here. The elevated window closes itself when it is done, and its exit code comes back to this one.
elevation.step.reports.title: Both reports land side by side.
elevation.measureNote: A scan can measure these sections without administrator rights. It cannot clear them.
elevation.smartScreenSummary: Windows may warn you the first time you install this
elevation.smartScreenWhy: The installer is not signed with a paid code-signing certificate, so Microsoft SmartScreen shows “Windows protected your PC” on first run. That is a statement about the certificate, not about the file.
elevation.smartScreenHow: Choose More info and then Run anyway. You can verify what you downloaded first: every release publishes a SHA-256 checksum for each installer, and a minisign signature the app’s own updater checks. Neither is a code-signing certificate - they prove the file is the one that was built, not who built it. The source is public.
elevation.smartScreenWhyHere: This note is here rather than hidden because meeting that dialog unexplained is worse than reading about it in advance.
